To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

interpretability is a key factor to consider when building predictive models; the proposed definition of interpretability is a rigorous mathematical framework that allows fair comparisons between any algorithms; the proposed interpretability measure is easy to compute and to understand; the proposed measure can be used as an optimization criterion in the design of new algorithms; the proposed measure has been used to compare four rule-based algorithms, which shows that it can be applied in practice.
interpretability is a concept that can be rigorously defined and quantitatively measured.
the interpretability of the algorithms is as follows: C4.5 < J48 < RIPPER < PART.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of an original and rigorous definition of the concept interpretability, which allows fair comparisons between rule-based algorithms, and its application to the comparison of four rule-based algorithms: J48, JRip, PART and OneR.
the development of a new method to compare the interpretability of rule based algorithms.
the definition of a rigorous mathematical definition for the interpretability of predictive algorithms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
C4.5 and RIPPER are more interpretable than CART and PART.
the C4.5 algorithm is the most interpretable algorithm.
the interpretability of the rules generated by the C4.5 algorithm is higher than the interpretability of those generated by the C5.0, the PART and the RIPPER algorithms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have defined interpretability of any algorithm in a rigorous mathematical way, allowing fair comparison between them.
interpretability is not a single property but a set of three properties: predictivity, simplicity and stability, each property can be defined mathematically and can be measured quantitatively.
we have provided a new definition and a new way of measuring the interpretability for rule-based algorithms.
The main takeaway from our work is that
interpretability is not only a function of the algorithm itself, but also of the dataset.
interpretability is a very important concept that should be considered when selecting the most suitable algorithm for a given problem.
the proposed interpretability measure allows to make fair comparisons between different algorithms, even when they do not generate the same number of rules.
